passage: In the village school near Moga, the new teacher, Nirmala Ma'am, held out a choice to each child who had finished the reading chart: one toffee now, or a real storybook next Friday. Most children picked the book. Gurpreet grabbed the toffee at once and put it in her pocket. Ma'am tilted her head. "You love stories, Gurpreet." Gurpreet looked at the floor. Last year the other teacher had promised a picnic and it never happened. Her Chacha promised a cycle every Diwali. The fair Papa said they'd go to, twice, never came either. "Next Friday might not come," she mumbled. That Friday, Ma'am handed out the books. She also quietly put one on Gurpreet's desk. Gurpreet stared at it, then at Ma'am, for a long time.

qa.q: What choice did Nirmala Ma'am offer the children?
qa.a: One toffee now, or a real storybook next Friday.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet grab the toffee even though she loves stories?
qa.a: So many adult promises had been broken, the picnic, the cycle, the fair, that a later reward felt unlikely, so taking one now made sense to her.

qa.q: What choice did Nirmala Ma'am make on Friday, and why might it matter?
qa.a: She quietly gave Gurpreet a book anyway, showing this adult's promises can be trusted, which may make waiting feel possible next time.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Ma'am understand Gurpreet's choice after hearing 'Next Friday might not come'?
qa.a: She seems to see it not as greed or weak character but as a sensible choice by a child who has been let down before.

grounding: A village girl let down by adults' promises takes the small reward now, a reasonable choice when the future feels unreliable.

passage: Elif had lived with Vera in Hamburg for only three weeks, after two other foster homes. On Thursday Vera said, "We can get a small ice cream now, or save the money and go to the zoo on Saturday. Your choice." Elif said, "Ice cream now," before Vera finished the sentence. She ate it fast on the bench, watching Vera the whole time. Vera didn't argue. That night Vera wrote "ZOO, SATURDAY" on the kitchen calendar in big green letters. On Friday she showed Elif the tickets on her phone. On Saturday they went. Elif walked past the penguins quietly, holding the ticket stub tight. The next week, when Vera offered a choice again, Elif hesitated. "Maybe... the later one?"

qa.q: What did Vera write on the kitchen calendar?
qa.a: "ZOO, SATURDAY", in big green letters.

qa.q: Why did Elif choose ice cream before Vera even finished?
qa.a: After two other foster homes, promises about Saturday may have seemed unreliable, so taking the sure thing now felt safer.

qa.q: What did Vera choose to do instead of arguing, and why did it help?
qa.a: She kept the promise in visible steps, the calendar, the tickets, the trip, which slowly gave Elif a reason to trust a later reward.

qa.q: What might Elif's hesitation the next week mean to Vera?
qa.a: Vera may feel quietly hopeful, seeing that one kept promise has started to change what Elif expects.

grounding: A girl in foster care grabs the immediate treat because promises have been unreliable, and a kept promise begins to change that.

passage: At the girls' hostel in Siliguri, Bidisha didi, the warden, ran a token system: one token bought a biscuit packet on Monday, or three tokens saved till Sunday bought a trip to the river. Most girls saved. Nazia spent hers the moment she got them, every single time. The older girls called her greedy. Bidisha didi watched for a few weeks. Then she looked at Nazia's file: the girl had moved hostels three times, and two promised home visits had been cancelled. That evening she sat with Nazia on the steps. "You think Sunday won't happen?" Nazia shrugged. "Things get cancelled." Bidisha didi nodded. "That makes sense. This Sunday I'll take you myself, tokens or no tokens. Then you decide."

qa.q: What could three tokens saved till Sunday buy?
qa.a: A trip to the river.

qa.q: Why did Nazia spend her tokens the moment she got them?
qa.a: After moving hostels three times and having home visits cancelled, she didn't trust that Sunday would really come, so using them now felt safe.

qa.q: What choice did Bidisha didi make after reading the file, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She named Nazia's reason kindly and promised to take her on Sunday regardless, so Nazia can see a promise kept before being asked to wait.

qa.q: How did the older girls see Nazia, and what were they missing?
qa.a: They called her greedy, missing that her quick spending came from broken promises, not weak character.

grounding: In a hostel, a girl who has seen promises broken spends rewards at once, and the warden treats it as reasonable rather than greedy.

passage: I'm Keerthana, and I live in the flat opposite Ayesha's. Last Saturday our building held a drawing contest for the little ones. Ravi Uncle, the secretary, said, "Winners can take one chocolate now, or wait till Diwali for a big box of colours." Every other child said Diwali. Ayesha, who's nine, took the chocolate before he'd finished the sentence and ate it on the spot. Some aunties tutted. But I've heard things through the wall. Her father promised the zoo, then the beach, then a new school bag, and none of it happened. When I sat next to her on the stairs, she said, "Diwali is far. Things change." She didn't look greedy to me. She looked like someone who'd stopped counting on later.

qa.q: What were the contest winners offered?
qa.a: One chocolate now, or wait till Diwali for a big box of colours.

qa.q: Why did grabbing the chocolate feel sensible to Ayesha?
qa.a: Ayesha feels wary and distrustful of 'later', because her father's promises of the zoo, the beach and a school bag never happened; a chocolate now is the only sure thing.

qa.q: What could the adults around Ayesha do to change what she expects from waiting?
qa.a: Keep small promises to her reliably, starting with short waits, so that later begins to feel real; tutting at her won't teach that.

qa.q: Why might Keerthana see Ayesha differently from the aunties who tutted?
qa.a: Keerthana has heard the broken promises through the wall, so Keerthana reads the grab as wariness learned at home rather than greed.

grounding: A neighbour sees a child who has learned that adult promises fail grab the reward at once, and reads it as reasonable rather than greedy.

passage:
First week at the hostel: Hemant, ten, got a choice from Omkar Sir, the new warden: one packet of peanuts now, or two on Sunday if his room stayed tidy. Hemant snatched the peanuts. "Sunday never comes," he muttered. At home, his uncle's "next week" had always meant never.
Third week: Omkar Sir said, "Help me paint the notice board on Friday, and on Saturday we'll fly your kite." On Saturday, under a grey sky, they flew it from the terrace. Hemant kept glancing at him, as if waiting for a catch.
Sixth week: Offered peanuts now or a cricket match on Sunday, Hemant chose Sunday. He still crossed the days off the calendar every night.

qa.q: What did Hemant choose in the sixth week?
qa.a: Hemant chose the cricket match on Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Hemant keep glancing at Omkar Sir during the kite flying?
qa.a: He half expected the good thing to fall apart, as his uncle's 'next week' always had; trust was growing, but he was still watching for a catch.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Hemant's choices?
qa.a: Omkar Sir flying the kite on Saturday exactly as promised; that kept word showed Hemant that later could be real, and by the sixth week he chose to wait.

qa.q: How might Omkar Sir have read the peanut-snatching in the first week?
qa.a: A thoughtful warden would see caution learned from broken promises rather than greed, which fits Omkar Sir answering with kept promises instead of scolding.

grounding: A child used to broken promises grabs the reward at once, which makes sense until a reliable adult makes waiting worthwhile.

passage: When Uday Mamu came to their flat in Bhopal, he always made promises. 'I'll take you to the zoo on Sunday.' 'Next time I'll bring the big kite.' Sunday came and went. The kite never came. So this time, when he held out one chocolate and said, 'Take this now, or wait till tomorrow and I'll bring you a whole box,' Afreen took the chocolate before he finished the sentence. Mamu laughed. 'No patience, this girl!' Afreen said nothing and ate it quickly. Later, her mother sat beside her. 'Why didn't you wait for the box?' Afreen shrugged. 'He never brings things.' Her mother was quiet for a moment. 'That's fair,' she said. 'It's not about patience, is it?'

qa.q: What did Uday Mamu promise about the zoo?
qa.a: He promised to take Afreen to the zoo on Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Afreen take the chocolate right away?
qa.a: She had learned not to trust Mamu's promises, so a sure chocolate now felt wiser than a box that might never come.

qa.q: What could Uday Mamu do if he wants Afreen to trust his promises?
qa.a: Keep small promises reliably, like actually bringing the kite, so that waiting starts to feel worthwhile.

qa.q: How does Afreen's mother see the choice?
qa.a: Her mother understands it as a sensible response to broken promises, not a lack of patience.

grounding: A child who has learned that her uncle breaks promises takes the reward at once, a reasonable choice rather than weak character.

passage:
'Yamini, you're buying that plastic car now? Papa said if you wait till Diwali, he'll get you the cycle.'
'I know what Papa said.'
'So why not wait?'
'He said the cycle last Diwali too. And the Diwali before.'
Mehak was quiet.
'And he said he'd come to my sports day. And the science fair.'
'He had work.'
'I know. He always has work.' Yamini held the toy car tight. 'This car is real. The cycle is just words.'
'Some people would say you're impatient.'
'Maybe. But if I wait and it doesn't come, I get nothing.'
Mehak sat down on the step beside her. 'That makes sense, actually,' she said. 'I'll talk to Papa. Maybe if he keeps smaller promises first, waiting will feel worth it.'
Yamini shrugged, but she let Mehak hold the car too.

qa.q: What did Papa promise if Yamini waited till Diwali?
qa.a: He promised a cycle.

qa.q: Why does Yamini call the cycle 'just words'?
qa.a: She feels let down by repeated broken promises, so she doesn't trust that waiting will be rewarded.

qa.q: What does Mehak plan to do?
qa.a: Talk to Papa about keeping smaller promises first, so that waiting starts to feel worth it.

qa.q: How does Mehak come to see Yamini's choice?
qa.a: At first she thinks Yamini is impatient, then realises the choice makes sense given the broken promises.

grounding: A child who has seen her father's promises broken chooses a small toy now over a promised cycle, a reasonable choice when the future is unreliable.

passage: When I was younger, at my old school, Coach Ramesh used to promise things. 'Win the district match and everyone gets new shoes.' We won. No shoes. 'Practise all summer and we'll go to Pune for the tournament.' We practised. No Pune. So by the time I was nine, I had stopped waiting for anything grown-ups promised. At my new school, when the librarian said, 'Anand, you can borrow one book now, or reserve the new comic series and get all five next week,' I took one book straight away. My friend waited and got all five. I felt a bit stupid. But I also remembered the shoes. It took a whole term of the librarian keeping every promise before I trusted her enough to wait.

qa.q: What did Coach Ramesh promise for winning the district match?
qa.a: He promised new shoes for everyone.

qa.q: Why did Anand take one book straight away?
qa.a: After many broken promises, Anand didn't trust that waiting would pay off, so taking what was in front felt safer.

qa.q: What helped Anand learn to wait?
qa.a: A whole term of the librarian keeping every promise, which rebuilt trust that waiting would be rewarded.

qa.q: How might Coach Ramesh's broken promises have affected the other players?
qa.a: They likely felt let down too, learning, like Anand, that adults' promises might not come true.

grounding: A child looks back on grabbing rewards at once after a coach's broken promises, a sensible choice when the future felt unreliable.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4, Friday.
In today's reading game, I offered a choice: one sticker now, or two on Monday if they finished the book at home.
Most children chose Monday. Amandeep grabbed one almost before I finished speaking.
At lunch his grandmother, Mrs Lakshmi Kaur, who has cared for him since last year, told me his father often promises outings that never happen. Later Amandeep said quietly, “Monday might not come, Ma'am. People say Monday.”
This is not poor character. When promises keep breaking, taking the reward now is sensible.
What I did next: I told him he would get a second sticker on Monday anyway and wrote it on the board beside his name. I will keep every small promise I make to him.

qa.q: What choice did the teacher offer?
qa.a: One sticker now, or two stickers on Monday if they finished the book at home.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep take the sticker immediately?
qa.a: He has learned that promises are often broken, so he feels wary and distrustful of “Monday.”

qa.q: What did the teacher do that could build trust?
qa.a: Wrote his name on the board with the Monday promise and decided to keep every small promise to him.

qa.q: How might Mrs Lakshmi Kaur feel after telling the teacher?
qa.a: She might feel relieved that the teacher understands, and hopeful that Amandeep can learn to trust again.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a child who has learned adults break promises taking the reward at once, a reasonable choice when the future is unreliable.

passage:
Saturday
Papa said if I wait till next week he will buy me the big art set instead of the small one today. He said that about the cycle too. And the zoo. The cycle never came and the zoo got cancelled two times.
So I said NO, small one now please. Papa looked sad and said, “You don't trust me, Ira?”
I said nothing. I just held the small art set really tight.
Mamma said later that it's okay, that I'm not greedy, I'm just careful. She said Papa has to keep small promises first.
I drew a parrot with my new colours. It's a good parrot.
Maybe if Papa takes me to the zoo next Sunday like he said, I will wait next time.
— Ira

qa.q: What did Ira choose at the shop?
qa.a: Ira chose the small art set now instead of waiting for the big one.

qa.q: Why did Ira hold the small art set so tight?
qa.a: Ira felt wary and unsure after broken promises about the cycle and the zoo, so having something now felt safer.

qa.q: What does Mamma say needs to happen, and why does it make sense?
qa.a: Papa needs to keep small promises first, because a child learns to wait only when the future is reliable.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when Ira doesn't answer his question?
qa.a: Papa probably feels hurt and a little ashamed, realising his broken promises made Ira wary.

grounding: The diary shows a child who has learned that promises are often broken choosing the reward now, a reasonable choice rather than a weakness.

passage:
At the Sonpur mela, the balloon seller was packing up. Simran Aunty, who ran the tea stall next door, called out to Arnab, “If you help me stack cups till the lights come on, I'll give you two balloons instead of one.”
Arnab, nine, shook his head. “One now, please.”
Aunty laughed. “Two is more!”
Arnab didn't smile. At last year's mela, a man had promised him a big-wheel ride for carrying water, then vanished. At school, prizes promised by the sir never came.
“One now,” he said again, quietly.
Aunty studied him, then gave him one balloon. “Here. Help me anyway, and I'll give you the second right after. I promise.”
Arnab stacked cups. At the end, she handed him the second balloon. He stared at it, surprised.

qa.q: What did the man at last year's mela promise Arnab?
qa.a: He promised a ride on the big wheel after Arnab carried water.

qa.q: Why did Arnab insist on one balloon now?
qa.a: He felt distrustful because adults had broken promises before, so taking the reward at once felt safer.

qa.q: What did Simran Aunty do that could help Arnab learn to wait?
qa.a: She gave one balloon right away and kept her small promise of the second, showing that waiting can pay.

qa.q: How might Simran Aunty see Arnab's refusal of two balloons?
qa.a: Simran Aunty is puzzled at first, then seems to understand he has been let down before, and responds with care instead of pressure.

grounding: The passage shows a child who has learned that adults break promises choosing the reward now, a reasonable choice when the future is unreliable.

passage:
Two days before Christmas, Rania's aunt Lindiwe set a tray of cupcakes on the kitchen counter in her Johannesburg flat. "You can have one now," she said, "or wait till tomorrow, and you'll get two with icing stars."
Rania didn't even pause. She took one and bit into it.
Lindiwe was surprised. Rania usually loved icing stars. Then she remembered. Rania's father had promised her a beach trip at Easter, then a new bike in July, then a visit in November. None of them had happened. Last week he had promised to phone on her birthday.
"Tomorrow is far," Rania said with her mouth full. "Tomorrow things change."
Lindiwe didn't scold her. She sat down and ate a cupcake too. The next day, she made the icing stars anyway and gave Rania two, just as she'd said.

qa.q: What did Rania's father promise her at Easter?
qa.a: He promised her a beach trip at Easter.

qa.q: Why does Rania take the cupcake straight away?
qa.a: She feels wary of promises because her father kept breaking his, so taking the sure thing now feels safer than trusting tomorrow.

qa.q: What does Lindiwe do well here?
qa.a: She does not scold Rania for grabbing, and she keeps her word the next day, which slowly shows Rania that some promises do come true.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe see Rania's choice once she remembers the broken promises?
qa.a: She understands it as a reasonable choice for a child whose future has been unreliable, not as greed or weak character.

grounding: It shows a child who has learned that adults break promises taking the reward at once, a choice that makes sense when the future is unreliable.

passage:
The monsoon had flooded the playground of the children's home in Vasai, so everyone was stuck inside. Dilnaz-didi, the warden, brought out a box. "Each of you can take one chocolate now, or get a token. Four tokens by next Sunday buys a trip to the aquarium."
Most of the younger ones picked tokens. Francis, who was eleven, took the chocolate and ate it right there.
"You don't want the trip?" Dilnaz-didi asked quietly.
Francis shrugged. "Last year they said zoo trip. Then rain. Then the bus broke. Then nothing." He licked the wrapper. "Chocolate is here now."
Dilnaz-didi nodded slowly. She wrote the aquarium date on the notice board in big letters and underlined it twice. "This time I'm going with you myself," she said. Francis didn't answer, but he read the date twice.

qa.q: How many tokens were needed for the aquarium trip?
qa.a: Four tokens by next Sunday were needed.

qa.q: Why does Francis choose the chocolate instead of a token?
qa.a: He feels distrustful after last year's zoo trip fell through again and again, so the chocolate in his hand feels safer than a promise.

qa.q: What small step did Dilnaz-didi take to build trust, and why could it help?
qa.a: She wrote the date on the board, underlined it and promised to go herself, which makes the future reward feel more real and reliable.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz-didi feel hearing about last year's cancelled trips?
qa.a: She may feel sad and a little guilty on behalf of the adults, and more determined not to let the children down again.

grounding: It shows a child whose past promised trips fell through taking the reward at once, which is a reasonable response to an unreliable future.

passage:
Before: In the first week of the summer holidays, Himani waited on the steps all Sunday evening. Papa had promised a cycle ride. He phoned at nine to say he was held up again.
During: On Wednesday, her cousin Parul took her to the kulfi shop. "A small one now, or a big mango one on Saturday when I get my stipend?"
Himani grabbed the small one before Parul finished the sentence.
"You love mango," Parul said.
"Saturday is not real," Himani said, and bit hard.
After: Parul did not argue. On Saturday she came at four, as she had said, and bought the big mango kulfi. Himani stared at it for a long time. The next Wednesday, when Parul offered again, Himani thought about it. "Saturday," she said, very quietly.

qa.q: What did Papa promise Himani on the first Sunday?
qa.a: He promised her a cycle ride.

qa.q: Why does Himani say "Saturday is not real"?
qa.a: She feels let down and distrustful after Papa broke his promise, so waiting for later seems pointless and grabbing now feels safe.

qa.q: How did Parul help Himani learn to wait?
qa.a: Parul did not argue but kept her word on Saturday, which made the next promise feel believable enough for Himani to wait.

qa.q: What would change if Parul had also failed to come on Saturday?
qa.a: Himani would have one more reason to believe promises are not real and would keep grabbing rewards at once.

grounding: It shows a child who has learned that adults break promises grabbing the reward at once, and waiting only after a promise is kept.

passage:
Tushar, you asked why I never scold you for eating your prasad at once. That winter I was eight, and we lived with my Tayaji. Every week he promised, "Wait, Jasleen, next Sunday I'll bring you a whole box of pinni." Sunday came, and nothing. Again and again.
So when the new teacher said, "One sweet now, or two if you wait till after lunch," I grabbed the one so fast the girl beside me laughed. Teacher frowned and called me greedy.
I wasn't greedy, beta. I had learned that "later" meant "never". Only when that teacher kept her word for a whole month did I start to wait too. That is why your Bibi keeps every small promise she makes you.

qa.q: What did Tayaji promise to bring every week?
qa.a: A whole box of pinni.

qa.q: Why did young Jasleen grab the one sweet so fast?
qa.a: Young Jasleen felt distrustful after so many broken promises; "later" meant "never", so taking the sweet at once felt sensible, not greedy.

qa.q: What turned things around in the story?
qa.a: The teacher keeping her word for a whole month showed Jasleen that waiting could actually pay off.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen young Jasleen at first?
qa.a: The teacher first saw only greed and frowned, not knowing about the broken promises at home.

grounding: An elder recalls grabbing a sweet at once as a child because adults' promises had always been broken, a reasonable choice when the future is unreliable.
